chapters.title: Chapter 3: Central Bank Coordination and Divergence

lessons.title: Currency Wars, Swap Lines, and Dollar Funding Stress

body.text: Currency wars and dollar funding stress sound similar but pull in opposite directions. One is a fight over who can make their currency weaker. The other is a scramble for dollars so intense it makes the dollar stronger, and it is the reason central bank swap lines exist at all.

children.text: Currency Wars: A Fight to Be Weaker

The phrase "currency war" was popularized in September 2010 by Brazil's then Finance Minister Guido Mantega, who accused major economies, the US in particular, of deliberately weakening their currencies through quantitative easing to gain a trade advantage. The mechanism is straightforward: QE tends to weaken a currency, a weaker currency makes exports cheaper and more competitive, and other countries facing that competitive pressure are tempted to ease their own policy in response, weakening their currencies too. Taken to its logical end, everyone eases at once trying to stay competitive, which is itself one path into the kind of synchronized liquidity expansion covered earlier in this course.

South Korea and other Asian exporters competing with Japan
Global markets, other EM exporters worried about a wider devaluation cycle

children.text: Dollar Funding Stress: The Opposite Problem

body.text: A currency war is a fight over who can get weaker. Dollar funding stress is the opposite: a global scramble for dollars so intense that the dollar gets stronger, even as the Fed itself may be easing domestically. Banks and companies outside the US routinely hold dollar-denominated liabilities, trade finance, dollar bonds, that must be serviced regardless of what their local currency is doing. In a crisis, everyone tries to secure dollars at the same time, and the resulting shortage shows up as a much stronger dollar and severe stress in dollar funding markets, distinct from any deliberate policy choice.

children.text: The cross-currency basis swap is the clearest gauge of this stress. It measures the extra cost, above the normal interest rate differential, that a non-US bank pays to borrow dollars through the FX swap market instead of directly. In calm conditions this cost hovers near zero. When dollar funding is scarce, non-US banks are willing to pay a steep premium for dollars, and the basis swings sharply negative.

body.label: EUR/USD Cross-Currency Basis, March 2020 Stress
body.context: A widely cited approximate range during the acute dash-for-dollars phase of the COVID shock, compared to a level near zero in calm markets. This is exactly the kind of dollar funding stress swap lines are built to relieve.

children.text: Swap Lines: The Fed's Answer to a Dollar Shortage

A central bank liquidity swap line lets a foreign central bank borrow dollars from the Fed, using its own currency as collateral, and then lend those dollars on to banks in its own jurisdiction that are struggling to find them. It is a direct fix for a dollar funding shortage that does not require any single struggling bank to be individually bailed out. The Fed first used swap lines at scale during the 2008 crisis, made a standing network with five major central banks permanent in 2013, and expanded temporary swap lines to a wider group of countries again in March 2020 as the COVID dash for dollars intensified.

children.text: India's absence from the Fed's swap network is not an oversight; it is a direct reason India places so much weight on building its own forex reserves, as covered in the previous lesson. Without a standing dollar backstop from the Fed, the RBI has had to self-insure, largely through reserves, and through its own bilateral arrangements, such as a swap agreement with the Bank of Japan worth roughly $75 billion agreed in 2018, which exists specifically as a backstop should India ever need dollar liquidity support outside of its own reserves.

body.title: Two Countries, Same Shock, Different Backstops
body.scenario: During a severe global dollar funding squeeze, South Korea, which has periodically had access to a temporary Fed swap line, and India, which has not, both see their banking systems short of dollars.
body.prompt: How would you expect the pressure on each country's reserves and currency to differ, given this difference in access to a Fed backstop, and why does this matter for how much reserve buffer each country needs to hold?
body.modelAnswer: A country with access to a Fed swap line has a lender of last resort for dollars specifically, so it can meet a domestic dollar shortage without having to sell down its own reserves as aggressively, which cushions pressure on its currency during the squeeze. India, without that access, has no equivalent backstop from the Fed and must rely almost entirely on its own reserves and bilateral arrangements like the swap line with the Bank of Japan to meet the same kind of dollar demand. This is exactly why India has historically placed such a high priority on building a large reserve buffer relative to its economy: without a standing Fed swap line, self-insurance through reserves is the main tool available, whereas a country with swap line access can run with a comparatively thinner reserve cushion for the same level of protection.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: What is the key difference between a "currency war" and "dollar funding stress"?
options: They are two names for the same phenomenon
A currency war is countries competing to weaken their currencies; dollar funding stress is a global scramble for dollars that makes the dollar stronger
A currency war only happens during recessions, while dollar funding stress only happens during expansions
Dollar funding stress is caused exclusively by the PBOC
body.explanation: A currency war involves countries deliberately weakening their own currencies to gain a trade advantage. Dollar funding stress is the opposite dynamic: a scramble for dollars to meet dollar-denominated obligations, which pushes the dollar stronger even as it creates severe funding market stress, and which swap lines are specifically built to relieve.

points: A currency war is a competitive race to weaken currencies for trade advantage; dollar funding stress is the opposite dynamic, a scramble for dollars that strengthens the dollar even amid crisis.
The cross-currency basis swap, swinging sharply negative, is the clearest market signal of acute dollar funding stress.
Fed swap lines let foreign central banks borrow dollars directly and lend them on domestically, defusing a dollar shortage without individual bank bailouts.
India is not part of the Fed's standing or 2020 temporary swap line network, which is a direct reason it places such weight on building large forex reserves as self-insurance.
India's bilateral swap arrangement with the Bank of Japan, roughly $75 billion, is a backstop distinct from and smaller in scope than the Fed's own standing swap network.
